headline: Outgoing After 11: Full Moon Current Loads the Inlet, Bass Trail the Bait Downhill
subhead: Daytime fluke are scattered and sulking on warm flats, but the building moon is stacking bass, blues, and weakfish behind the bait after dark.
body_markdown:
Full moon hits tomorrow night, and if you're only getting one shot at Shinnecock this week, that's the tide to build around — not the flood, the outgoing, and not at dinnertime, somewhere past 11 PM when the current really starts hauling. That's the decision that matters more than which lure is in the bag right now. Daytime fishing in the bay has gone soft and spread out with the water sitting warm on the flats, and the fish that are still eating with any conviction are doing it on structure, in the dark, on the stronger half of the tide. We flagged this pattern building last week — said the current concentrating bait would intensify as the moon built toward full — and that's exactly what's setting up at the inlet mouth right now.

The mechanics are simple. Warm surface water on the bay flats pushes fluke and bass off the shallow structure during daylight, and they don't reconcentrate until that outgoing tide starts ripping bait out of the back creeks and marsh edges and funneling it through the inlet. The bigger the tidal swing, the harder that current runs, the tighter the bait gets squeezed against the rocks — and the bass know it. A full moon means bigger swings than we've had in weeks, and the fleet working after dark has noticed the difference already, with better numbers on the last two nights of outgoing than anything in the daylight bite.

Striped bass are the headline, and the program hasn't changed in years because it doesn't need to — fish the east jetty and the deep hole off the Coast Guard station on the back half of the outgoing, working bucktails in the 1.5 to 2-ounce range tipped with a strip of fluke belly or a white 5-inch Gulp swimming mullet, bounced slow along bottom where the current edge meets the deeper cut. Slot fish are mixed with a decent number of overslots holding in that deep hole, and the ones being kept in the legal window are mostly 26 to 32 inches. Live eels fished on a fish-finder rig, slow-trolled or drifted right along the rocks after dark, have been the most consistent producer for the bigger fish — this is not a lure most guys reach for until the sun goes down, and there's a reason for that. Bass in that inlet current get cagey in daylight and reckless after dark, which is the whole case for fishing nocturnal here in late August.

Bluefish are riding shotgun with the bass the way they have all month, chopping up peanut bunker schools that are getting pushed out of the back bay on the same outgoing water. Cocktail blues in the 3 to 5-pound range are showing up in the same drifts as the bass, and if you're throwing bucktails or Deadly Dicks along the jetty rocks, expect to lose a few to blue teeth before the night's over. Snapper blues are still thick up in the canal and around the docks in Hampton Bays, which tells you the adult fish still have plenty of forage to stay parked on before they start sliding out toward the ocean side for fall.

Weakfish are the one that rewards patience at Ponquogue Bridge. The pattern there hasn't moved — fish the shadow lines under the bridge lights on the last two hours of the outgoing, working a bucktail-and-Gulp combo or a bare jighead tipped with squid strips slow along the bottom where the current sweeps past the pilings. These aren't blitz fish. It's a handful of quality weakfish in the 3 to 5-pound class on a good night, more shorts than keepers most nights, but the ones coming over the rail have been solid, healthy fish, and the bridge remains the most reliable spot on the south shore for them this time of year.

Fluke are the tougher sell right now, and there's no point pretending otherwise. The warm, thin-oxygen water sitting on the open bay flats has scattered them out instead of holding them tight to structure, which is softening catch rates almost everywhere except the channel edges and the deeper cuts near the inlet where a cooler bottom layer still persists. If fluke are the target, work the deeper water drifting past Tiana Beach into the inlet throat on the last of the incoming, white or chartreuse bucktails with a Gulp trailer, keeping the boat moving slow enough to hug bottom in 15 to 25 feet. It's not a numbers game right now — it's a quality-over-quantity game, and the biggest fish are coming from the deepest, coolest water available.

Porgies remain a dependable bread-and-butter option inside the inlet on bloodworms or clam, fished on the bottom around the jetty rocks on either tide, and worth keeping in your back pocket if the bass and weakfish go quiet on a given night.

Looking ahead, the building moon should keep sharpening these outgoing-tide windows through the weekend, and if the wind stays out of the southwest in the 8 to 12-knot range as it has been, water clarity at the inlet should hold clean enough for the eel bite to keep producing after dark. Watch the tide change at the inlet mouth on calm mornings too — bait is tightening up out there, and it wouldn't be a surprise to see the first false albacore push through on that clean water before Labor Day. For now, the smart move is simple: sleep through the heat, fish the dark, and let the moon do the work.
